If S.c10 is NULL, no rows match (since NULL = NULL yields unknown), so COUNT(*) returns 0 and the row is returned. In Q2 the condition is written as 'WHERE NOT c10 IN (...)'. When c10 is NULL, even if the subquery returns non‐NULL values, the expression (NULL IN (...)) evaluates to unknown, and the NOT condition fails. Thus, a row in table3 with a NULL c10 can be returned by Q1 but not by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows into table3: one with c10 = NULL and one with c10 = a non-null value. Then insert a matching pair in table2/table1 so that the subquery produces a non-empty set. In Q1 the row with c10 = NULL will be returned (since the join condition never matches NULL), while in Q2 the NULL value causes the NOT IN predicate to evaluate to false, so that row is omitted.

In contrast, Q2 filters table3 rows based solely on their c6 value not appearing anywhere in a (LEFT JOIN based) subquery that finds any table3 row associated (via table2) with a table1 row having 'RED'. This means that if two different table3 rows share the same c6 value, one of them might qualify in Q1 (because its own c10 sees no matching table2/table1 record) while Q2 would exclude it because the other row (with a different c10) was linked to a table2/table1 record. Thus, their logic is not aligned.

Q1 looks at rows in table1 whose c2 is exactly one less or one more (i.e. O1.c2-1 or O1.c2+1) and then checks if that row’s c1 is 1; whereas Q2, after computing window functions, checks if the current row’s c1 equals the immediately preceding or following row’s c1 (in an unspecified but fixed order, which if assumed to be by c2 is still only positional, not arithmetic with difference 1). In effect, Q1 demands an arithmetic gap of 1 between the c2 values while Q2 merely compares adjacent rows in the computed order. For instance, if one inserts rows with (c2, c1) = (1,1) and (3,1), Q1 will find no row with c2 exactly equal to 0,2 or 4 (so no neighbors), but Q2 (when ordered by c2) will treat these two rows as adjacent and return both.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT P.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS DP ON P.c1 = DP.c1 WHERE P.c2 <> DP.c2
explanation: Q1 groups rows by c1 and returns those groups with more than one occurrence (i.e. duplicate c1 values). Q2 self-joins table1 on c1 and, via the condition P.c2 <> DP.c2, ensures that there exist two distinct rows (distinct primary keys c2) with the same c1. Because c2 is a primary key (hence unique), any duplicate c1 must appear in rows with different c2 values. Thus, both queries return the same set of c1 values that occur more than once.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(A.c1 - B.c1) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A CROSS JOIN table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 > B.c1
explanation: Both queries attempt to compute the smallest difference between two distinct values in table1. Q1 evaluates all pairs where A.c1 != B.c1 and then takes the absolute difference using ABS(A.c1 - B.c1), ensuring symmetry. Q2 restricts to pairs with A.c1 > B.c1 so the difference (A.c1 - B.c1) is already positive. In effect, Q2 finds the minimum positive gap between any two values. Since every unordered pair appears in Q1 twice (once in each order) and one ordering meets the condition A.c1 > B.c1 in Q2, the two queries are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT P.c2, P.c1, COALESCE(SUM(AMOUNT), 0) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, COUNT(c3) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM (SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'DESKTOP' AS c1 FROM table1 UNION SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'MOBILE' AS c1 FROM table1 UNION SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'BOTH' AS c1 FROM table1) AS P LEFT JOIN (SELECT c2, c3, CASE WHEN MOBILE_AMOUNT > 0 THEN CASE WHEN DESKTOP_AMOUNT > 0 THEN 'BOTH' ELSE 'MOBILE' END ELSE 'DESKTOP' END AS c1, (MOBILE_AMOUNT + DESKTOP_AMOUNT) AS AMOUNT FROM (SELECT c2, c3, SUM(CASE c1 WHEN 'MOBILE' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS MOBILE_AMOUNT, SUM(CASE c1 WHEN 'DESKTOP' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS DESKTOP_AMOUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c2, c3) AS O) AS T ON P.c1 = T.c1 AND P.c2 = T.c2 GROUP BY c2, c1
q2: WITH CTE AS (SELECT c3, c2, SUM(CASE WHEN c1 = 'MOBILE' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS MA, SUM(CASE WHEN c1 = 'DESKTOP' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS DA FROM table1 GROUP BY c3, c2) SELECT c2, 'DESKTOP' AS c1, SUM(CASE WHEN CTE.DA > 0 AND CTE.MA = 0 THEN DA ELSE 0 END) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, SUM(CASE WHEN CTE.DA > 0 AND CTE.MA = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM CTE GROUP BY c2 UNION ALL SELECT c2, 'MOBILE' AS c1, SUM(CASE WHEN CTE.DA = 0 AND CTE.MA > 0 THEN MA ELSE 0 END) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, SUM(CASE WHEN CTE.DA = 0 AND CTE.MA > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM CTE GROUP BY c2 UNION ALL SELECT c2, 'BOTH' AS c1, SUM(CASE WHEN CTE.DA > 0 AND CTE.MA > 0 THEN DA + MA ELSE 0 END) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, SUM(CASE WHEN CTE.DA > 0 AND CTE.MA > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM CTE GROUP BY c2
explanation: Both queries are written to compute, for each distinct date (c2) in table1 and for each of the three possible channel labels (DESKTOP, MOBILE, BOTH), the total amount (which is the sum of AMOUNTs for that date and channel) and the number of users (identified by c3) having that channel classification. In Q1 a derived table (P) is built by taking each c2 from table1 and pairing it with the three channel labels. A second derived table (T) aggregates table1 by (c2, c3) to compute sums for MOBILE and DESKTOP amounts and then assigns a classification (‘DESKTOP’ if only DESKTOP exists, ‘MOBILE’ if only MOBILE exists, and ‘BOTH’ if both exist). The LEFT JOIN on c2 and channel then ensures that for every date and every channel candidate—even if no users fall into that category—a row is produced (with 0 sums and counts when there is no match). In Q2 a CTE aggregates table1 per user (c3) and date (c2) into MOBILE and DESKTOP amounts. Then three UNION ALL subqueries, each grouping by c2 and filtering by the specific condition on the aggregated amounts (only DESKTOP, only MOBILE, or BOTH), compute the total amounts and total user counts. Thus, in essence both queries are using the exact same grouping and classification logic, even though one is written with a LEFT JOIN over a generated candidate set and the other with UNION ALL over condition‐filtered aggregations. Therefore the two queries are semantically equivalent.

The DISTINCT in Q2 (both in the outer SELECT and in the subquery) is redundant because the GROUP BY already ensures distinct groups and the IN clause ignores duplicates. However, if any row in table2 has c1 = NULL, the subquery in Q1 returns a set that includes a NULL value, causing the NOT IN check to evaluate to UNKNOWN for every row (and thus filter out all rows). In contrast, Q2 builds its subquery by joining table1 and table2 using the condition table2.c1 = table1.c2. When table2.c1 is NULL the join condition is false, so that row is excluded, and the subquery never returns NULL. As a result, in the presence of a NULL in table2.c1 the two queries can yield different results.

Q1 does this by filtering table1 with a subquery (c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1)) and grouping by c1. Q2 does it by joining table1 to itself on F1.c1 = F2.c2 and then, for each F2.c2 that is common, counting the distinct F1.c2 values (which by the primary key constraint are as many as there are rows with c1 = X). Thus, under the given schema constraints, they are semantically equivalent.

Under SQL’s semantics, they return the same result.
